near_miss.lead: Life or limbs as a legal merism
near_miss.why_not: Corpus search confirms the Norse legal binomial, but no cross-branch counterpart was found. Slab partners concern enemies/friends and cosmic light, not this merism.

near_miss.lead: Killing mother, father, sister as a catalogue of crimes
near_miss.why_not: AVP 19.46.s26 and the Norse law share kin terms and condemnation of kin-killing, but differ in order, syntax (agent compounds versus finite verbs), verb roots and scope. Searches found only this AVP line and epic discussions of killing parents. The natural enumeration of closest relatives does not establish inherited phrasing.

near_miss.why_not: The slab partners do not supply the same eye/sun metaphor: Armenian is a Christian fountain of light, Latin concerns grafting buds, Sanskrit knowing a friend. External Vedic comparison recorded separately.

search_lead.cognate: Norse sol (sól) and Sanskrit sūryaḥ continue the Indo-European sun word; auga and cakṣus are lexical renewal, not cognates.
search_lead.argument: Norse poetic instruction permits calling the eye the sun; the Vedic predication identifies the sun with the speaker’s eye. This inversely directed eye/sun correspondence merits comparison, but a late metapoetic catalogue and a Vedic bodily-cosmic identification are not by themselves proof of inheritance.

near_miss.lead: Keeping words in a royal agreement and administering oaths
near_miss.why_not: Norse hostage-return condition and Old Russian oath administration have comparable treaty settings but neither a shared lexical pair nor matching syntactic figure.

near_miss.lead: Truth versus falsehood in reported knowledge
near_miss.why_not: Norse truthful reporting contrasted with lying and Russian uncertainty whether a report is true or false are ordinary epistemic alternatives; no distinctive inherited wording established.

near_miss.lead: Spring and movement / Venus and working
near_miss.why_not: Norse men come in spring to cultivate land; Latin Spring and Venus advance in a personified seasonal procession. Spring is an adjunct in Norse and a moving subject in Latin, so the apparent cluster has no shared phrase.

near_miss.lead: Mother and father in identity and naming
near_miss.why_not: Irish mother/father/name unknown and Homeric parents naming the speaker share ordinary identity vocabulary, but not a marked collocation or congruent naming act. Norse maternal grandfather gives his name; the other partners have genealogies, death or parents slain. No inherited formula established.

Norse ausa vatni refers to sprinkling a newborn in the preceding/following context. Homeric ἀφυσσάμεθ’ ὕδωρ is drawing water for voyagers, not naming or adoption; functional and lexical differences prevent an inherited collocation claim.

near_miss.lead: Flower of age / new poetic flowers
near_miss.why_not: Lucretius 1.928 refers to newly gathered poetic flowers, whereas the Norse age-genitive marks youthful flourishing contrasted with old age. Search found closer external age-genitives, recorded separately.

search_lead.cognate: Norse bloma (blómi, dative singular) and Latin florem (flos, accusative singular) share the flowering root *bʰleh₃-; aldrs/aetatis are not asserted cognate. Greek supplies a semantic parallel.
search_lead.argument: Norse bloma aldrs and Latin aetatis florem both construe prime of life as flower plus age genitive; Homer’s youth-genitive offers a third tradition. The slab Latin partner has only literal/poetic flowers. Medieval Latin influence or independent metaphor remains possible, so the external comparison needs review rather than a slab-anchored claim.

near_miss.why_not: Norse fecc conu and Armenian առնուլ կին denote obtaining/marrying a wife; the Greek partners use marriage or possession. Wife/daughter kin terms are cognate, but the verbs and syntax differ, and royal marriage genealogy is routine.

near_miss.lead: Silence and not uttering a word
near_miss.why_not: Norse no one gets a word from Rǿrekr and Latin a door never mutters a word share cognate word vocabulary, but different constructions and comic versus human contexts; negated speech is too ordinary to demonstrate inheritance.

near_miss.lead: Heroic armour shining like stars and fire in preceding context
near_miss.why_not: The Norse context compares helmet and arms to stars, gold and fire. None of its three assigned partners describes luminous armour; a Greek helmet/star lemma-pair search returned no hit. A widespread glittering-armour image without a verified cognate collocation does not support a claim.

Both tongue and heart are cognate with the AV organs, but the Norse grammatical treatise explains a rhetorical figure, whereas AVŚ 5.29 orders the demon’s organs pierced. Greek searches chiefly returned anatomy and Christian/moral heart-tongue contrasts, not the same inherited phrase. Learned transmission is an immediate alternative.

near_miss.lead: Gold as fire of water/rivers in preceding context
near_miss.why_not: Vedic search found fire held as an embryo by waters and fires in waters, but no identification of gold by the Norse kenning. The relevant fire and water nouns are not a demonstrated cognate pair here; Greek slab partners concern military affairs. Mythic resemblance alone is insufficient.

near_miss.lead: Loving a person like one’s eyes
near_miss.why_not: Greek assigned partners discuss courage, understanding and military preparation; neither contains the affection/eyes comparison. Closer Latin parallels were found externally and are recorded as a search lead.

search_lead.cognate: Norse augunum (auga, dative plural) and Latin oculis (oculus, ablative plural) continue the eye root *h₃ekʷ-. Unna and amo are not asserted cognate.
search_lead.argument: The Norse ann henni sem augunum compares a husband’s love for his wife with his own eyes; Catullus compares affection for a sparrow and a friend with one’s own eyes. Both use a verb of love and a possessively anchored eye comparison, Latin with greater-than rather than equality. This striking valuation formula merits review, but independent idiom and medieval transmission remain possible.
